passages.t: The sons of Japheth: the far coastlands
passages.happening:
A new section begins: “This is the account of Noah’s sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, who also had sons after the flood” (verse 1).

First come the sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras (verse 2). Then the sons of Gomer and of Javan, among them Tarshish and the Kittites (verses 3-4).

“From these, the maritime peoples separated into their territories, according to their languages, by clans within their nations” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is often called the Table of Nations. It is a map in the form of a family tree. The names are of people, but many of them are also names of peoples and places the first hearers knew.

Some can be matched with peoples known from ancient records. Madai is the Medes, in what is now Iran. Javan is the Ionians, the Greeks. Gomer is usually linked with a people the Assyrians called the Gimirrai, the Cimmerians. Tubal and Meshech were peoples to the north. Kittim points to Cyprus, and Tarshish to a far port across the Mediterranean Sea, the place Jonah tried to flee to (Jonah 1:3). Some names cannot now be placed with any certainty.

For an Israelite, these were the distant peoples of the north and west, over the sea and on the islands. They are named first, and briefly. Genesis often deals with the side branches first and the main line last. Shem's line, which the story will follow, comes at the end.

Notice the phrase ‘according to their languages’. Different languages are already part of the picture here. Chapter 11 will tell how that came about. The two chapters are arranged by theme, not strictly by time.
passages.later:
Many of these far-off names return in the prophets as the ends of the earth that God will reach. Isaiah says God will send messengers “to Tarshish, Put, and the archers of Lud; to Tubal, Javan, and the islands far away who have not heard of My fame or seen My glory” (Isaiah 66:19).

Ezekiel names “Gog of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal” as a far northern enemy (Ezekiel 38:2), and Revelation uses Gog and Magog as names for the nations gathered against God (Revelation 20:8).
passages.asks: The list begins with people far from Israel, over the sea. Ask who seems far away to you: far in place, in language or in culture. Then notice that God names them in Scripture before Israel even exists. Ask what it means that the God you worship knew their names first.

passages.t: The sons of Ham, Nimrod, and Canaan
passages.happening:
The sons of Ham are Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan (verse 6). The sons of Cush are listed, among them Sheba and Dedan (verse 7).

Cush is the father of Nimrod, “who began to be a mighty one on the earth” (verse 8). He was “a mighty hunter before the LORD” (verse 9). His kingdom began in Babylon, Erech and Accad, in the land of Shinar (verse 10). From there he went into Assyria, where he built Nineveh and Calah (verses 11-12).

Mizraim is the father of several peoples, among them the Casluhites, “from whom the Philistines came” (verses 13-14). Canaan is the father of Sidon and of the peoples of the land: Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites and others (verses 15-18). The borders of Canaan ran from Sidon to Gaza and toward Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Some of these names are plain. Mizraim is the ordinary Hebrew word for Egypt. Cush is the land south of Egypt along the Nile, often called Ethiopia in older Bibles. Put was probably Libya, in north Africa. Sheba and Dedan were peoples of Arabia.

Nimrod is given a short story of his own. He is the first person called a ‘mighty one’ after the flood. The same word was used for the ‘mighty men of old’ before it (6:4). He is a hunter and a builder of kingdoms. His cities are the great cities of Mesopotamia: Babylon, Erech (the city of Uruk) and Accad in the south, and Nineveh and Calah, later the capitals of Assyria. The first hearers would hear the names of the empires that one day would crush Israel. Scholars have suggested several real kings or legends behind Nimrod, but none has been proved.

The Philistines appear as descendants of Egypt's line. Elsewhere the Bible says they came from Caphtor (Amos 9:7), usually taken to be Crete.

Canaan's descendants are the peoples of the land God would promise to Abraham. Verse 19 draws its borders. For Israel, this was home.
passages.later:
The prophets look forward to a day when even Israel's great enemies will belong to God. Isaiah hears God say, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). A psalm names Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush among “those who know Me” (Psalm 87:4).

Micah calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod” (Micah 5:6). Nimrod's kingdoms became a byword for the power of empire.

On the day of Pentecost, Luke lists people from many of these lands hearing the gospel in their own languages: “Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene”, and “Cretans and Arabs” (Acts 2:10-11).
passages.hard:
Does this list rank the peoples, or say anything about race? No.

The list is not a modern table of races or languages. It groups peoples by land, by history and by political ties, as much as by descent. Canaan, whose people spoke a language very close to Hebrew, is listed under Ham. Elam, whose language was not related to Hebrew, is listed under Shem. The chapter places every people, including Israel's worst enemies, in one family descended from Noah.

Nothing here says that any people is higher or lower than another, or cursed by birth. Ham's line includes Egypt, a great kingdom, and Cush, and Babylon and Nineveh through Nimrod. The so-called ‘curse of Ham’, used to defend slavery, has no ground in this chapter, as it has none in chapter 9.
passages.asks: Nimrod built great cities, and his name became a picture of empire. Ask what you are building, and whether it is for your own name or for God's. Then think about a people you have been taught to see as an enemy. Ask what it would mean to read Isaiah's ‘Blessed be Egypt My people’ with their name in it.

passages.t: The sons of Shem, and one family of nations
passages.happening:
Sons were also born to Shem, “the forefather of all the sons of Eber” (verse 21). The sons of Shem are Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram (verse 22). The line runs through Arphaxad and Shelah to Eber (verse 24).

Eber has two sons. “One was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided, and his brother was named Joktan” (verse 25). Joktan's thirteen sons are listed (verses 26-29). Their land stretched “from Mesha to Sephar, in the eastern hill country” (verse 30).

The chapter closes: “All these are the clans of Noah’s sons, according to their generations and nations. From these the nations of the earth spread out after the flood” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Some of Shem's sons are well known. Elam lay east of Babylon. Asshur is the ordinary Hebrew name for Assyria. Aram is the Arameans of Syria.

Eber is named with care. His name may lie behind the word ‘Hebrew’, though that is not certain. The story will follow his line to Abraham (11:14-26).

Peleg's name sounds like the verb ‘to divide’. In his days ‘the earth was divided’. Most readers take this as the scattering at Babel in the next chapter. Others think of a division of land or of Eber's family into two branches. The text gives no more.

The phrase ‘clans, languages, lands, and nations’ ends each part of the chapter (verses 5, 20 and 31). Every people has its own language and land, and all come from one family. The word for ‘clans’ is the word God will use when he promises Abraham that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The families listed here are the ones that promise has in view.
passages.later:
Paul told the people of Athens, “From one man He made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands” (Acts 17:26).

Jesus sends his followers to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). And the Bible's last vision gathers the scattered families back together: “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9).
passages.hard:
How many nations are there? By the usual count, the Hebrew list holds seventy names; the ancient Greek translation has seventy-two. Later Jewish teaching spoke of the seventy nations of the world. Many readers think the number is meant to say ‘all the nations’, a number of fullness. Seventy is also the number of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:27), which some see as Israel standing for the world in small.

When Jesus sends out a larger group of followers in Luke, the number is seventy-two in the Berean Standard Bible (Luke 10:1), and seventy in some ancient copies and other Bibles. Some readers link that number with the nations of Genesis 10, a mission that points to the whole world. Others think the link is uncertain. These notes do not decide.
passages.asks: Every people on earth is in this one family. Ask whether you treat people of other nations and languages as family, or as strangers. Then remember God's promise to bless ‘all the families of the earth’. Ask what part you could play in that blessing reaching someone far from you.
